passage:
Wednesday
Papa found out I'd filled in the form for the arts stream and not science. He didn't shout. He said, very quietly, "If you do this, don't tell anyone you're my daughter. The whole family will be laughed at." Then he went to his room. Ma sat with me and said, "He only wants your good. You know how much he loves you."
And he does. He wakes at five to drop me at tuition. He saved for years for my laptop. That's what makes it so confusing. The same person who loves me is the one making me feel ashamed of the thing I actually want.
Bhupen-dada came in later and sat on the floor. He said, "You're allowed to love him and still want your own life." I cried into my pillow after he left.
I haven't torn up the form. Tomorrow I'll ask Mrs Kharkongor if she can talk to us together.
Minakshi

qa.q: Which stream had Minakshi filled in the form for?
qa.a: The arts stream, not science.

qa.q: Why does Minakshi feel so confused?
qa.a: Minakshi feels torn and ashamed, because the same Papa who loves her and wakes at five for her is the one threatening shame over what she wants.

qa.q: What small step is Minakshi planning, and why might it help?
qa.a: Asking Mrs Kharkongor to talk to the family together brings in a respected outside adult who can help the conversation without it becoming a fight.

qa.q: How does Bhupen-dada see Minakshi's situation?
qa.a: Bhupen-dada seems to understand the pull of both love and freedom, telling Minakshi it is allowed to love Papa and still want her own life.

grounding: Shows a young person whose loving family controls her choice of study with the threat of shame, leaving her torn between love and freedom.

passage: The last bus to Rohtak left in twenty minutes, and Jagdish was still in the practice room behind the music shop, changing out of the band T-shirt he'd worn for his friend Sumit's gig. He folded it into the bottom of his bag, under the ironed shirt his mother liked. At home he'd say he had been at the library. "Why do you do this?" Sumit asked, handing him a comb. "They'd never throw you out." "No," Jagdish said. "They'd just go quiet. Papa would sigh for a week, and Ma would tell Chachi I've changed." He ran for the bus stop in the rain, heart thudding, rehearsing library details. On the bus he texted Sumit: "Maybe I'm living two lives." Sumit replied: "You are. Remember Mehra sir from school? Your dad respects him. Maybe talk to him first?" Jagdish stared at the wet window and, for once, didn't push the idea away.

qa.q: What did Jagdish plan to say at home about where he had been?
qa.a: He'd say he had been at the library.

qa.q: How does Jagdish feel on the bus?
qa.a: Jagdish feels anxious and split in two, heart thudding and rehearsing library details, and admits he may be living two lives.

qa.q: What first step is suggested, and why might it help?
qa.a: Naming the pattern and talking to Mehra sir, whom his father respects, could help Jagdish be honest at home without losing the family's warmth.

qa.q: How does Sumit see Jagdish's hiding?
qa.a: Sumit calls it two lives and believes the family would never throw Jagdish out, so he gently pushes him toward honesty with an elder's help.

grounding: Shows a loved young adult who hides and performs to avoid losing family approval, and is nudged to name the pattern and seek a respected elder.

passage: You think I always got along with your Nana and Nani, Ishita? Not at all. When I was twenty-five, I got a teaching job in Shillong, and they wanted me to stay in Jaipur and marry the boy they had chosen. There was shouting. Your Nana said I'd be no daughter of his. I was frightened, but I didn't shout back. One evening I sat with them and said, "I love you. I'm taking the job. I'll decide who I marry. And I'll come home every Diwali." Then I did exactly that. The first Diwali, Nana barely spoke. The second, he asked about my students. By the fourth, he was sending me pickle. My friend Leela had it worse: her brothers threatened to lock her in, so she moved to a women's hostel with a counsellor's help. Different homes need different steps, beta. But calm words and kept promises, that is what worked for your Rekha maasi.

qa.q: Where did Rekha get a teaching job?
qa.a: In Shillong.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel when Nana said she'd be no daughter of his?
qa.a: Rekha felt frightened, but stayed calm and chose not to shout back.

qa.q: Which choice in the story kept the relationship alive?
qa.a: Rekha said calmly what she would decide herself and kept her promise to come home every Diwali, so affection and contact continued.

qa.q: How did Nana's feelings seem to change over the Diwalis?
qa.a: Nana went from barely speaking, to asking about her students, to sending pickle, suggesting his anger softened as she kept coming back.

grounding: Shows an adult child calmly stating what she will decide and keeping contact with family, while a friend facing threats needed outside help and a safe hostel.

passage: At the kindergarten in Busan, Ms Leila sat the children on the rug beside a drawing of a child in a swimsuit. "The parts under your swimsuit are private," she said. "Nobody should touch them or ask to see them." Soo-ah raised her hand. "Not even a nice grown-up?" "Not even a nice one. And a grown-up should never ask you to keep a secret from Mum or Dad. Surprises, like a birthday present, are fine, because everyone finds out soon." They practised saying, "No! I'm telling!" in big voices. Soo-ah shouted loudest, then giggled.

qa.q: What did the children practise saying?
qa.a: They practised saying “No! I'm telling!” in big voices.

qa.q: How did Soo-ah seem to feel while practising?
qa.a: Soo-ah seemed confident and cheerful, shouting loudest and then giggling, so the rule felt safe rather than scary.

qa.q: Why is teaching the rules with practice better than frightening stories?
qa.a: Simple rules repeated and practised playfully help children remember what to do and whom to tell, without making them afraid.

qa.q: How might Soo-ah's parents feel hearing about the lesson?
qa.a: They might feel reassured and grateful, knowing Soo-ah learned that grown-ups should not ask for secrets from Mum or Dad and that telling is always allowed.

grounding: Shows an adult teaching young children that private parts are private, that grown-ups should not ask for secrets from parents, and that telling is always allowed.

passage: At the recharge shop in the village, Amandeep-uncle always had a toffee ready for Naveen. Lately he let Naveen play games on his phone in the back room, and gave him a shiny cricket cap. "You're my favourite," he said. "Our special game is a secret, okay?" Naveen felt proud and grown-up, but his tummy felt odd as he walked home. That evening Dadi saw the cap. "Who gave this, beta?" Naveen looked at his feet. "It's a secret." Dadi put down the rolling pin and sat beside him. "You did right to tell me. Grown-ups shouldn't ask children for secrets from family. You're not in trouble." Before dinner she had called Naveen's father home and phoned the head of the village child protection committee.

qa.q: What did Amandeep-uncle give Naveen?
qa.a: A toffee and a shiny cricket cap, and he let Naveen play games on his phone.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel about the special attention?
qa.a: Naveen felt proud and grown-up, yet his tummy felt odd on the way home, a sign he was confused.

qa.q: How did Dadi respond, and why was it right?
qa.a: She stayed calm, said Naveen did right and was not in trouble, and called his father and the child protection committee the same evening, protecting him without scaring him.

qa.q: How might Dadi have felt when Naveen said the cap was a secret?
qa.a: Dadi likely felt alarmed and protective, but she kept her worry quiet, stayed calm with Naveen and acted before dinner.

grounding: Shows a child given gifts, phone games and a secret by an adult, feeling important but uneasy, and a grandmother who responds calmly the same day.

passage:
Saturday
Today I told Papa about Coach Vinod. How he gives me chocolates after swimming, and said our talks are a secret, and last week wanted me to stay late alone. I thought Papa would be angry with me for keeping it. He wasn't. He put his tea down and said, "Thank you for telling me, Kashish. I believe you. You did nothing wrong." His voice was soft even though his hands were tight. Then he called Mummy and Mr Shankar, the swimming club's head, and after lunch we all went there together. I don't have to go to class with Coach Vinod anymore. Papa said I can tell him anything, always, and he won't get cross.
I feel lighter.

qa.q: What did Coach Vinod give Kashish after swimming?
qa.a: Chocolates.

qa.q: What was Kashish afraid of before telling Papa?
qa.a: Kashish was afraid Papa would be angry about the secret, and afterwards felt lighter and relieved.

qa.q: What did Papa do that made telling safe?
qa.a: He stayed calm, thanked Kashish, said he believed it and that Kashish did nothing wrong, then called Mummy and Mr Shankar and went to the club the same day.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt inside while staying calm?
qa.a: Papa's tight hands suggest he felt angry and worried, but he kept his voice soft so Kashish would not feel blamed.

grounding: Shows a parent who hears a child mention gifts, a secret and pressure to stay alone, stays calm, believes and thanks the child, and acts to protect the same day.

passage:
Week 1, Monday: Wasim-sir, the young man who ran the online art class, messaged Parveen after the session: "Your sketches are special. You're more mature than the others." She read it three times, smiling.
Week 3, Friday: Their chats had moved to a private app. "Your parents wouldn't get our friendship," he wrote. "Delete these, okay? It's just ours." Parveen had stopped telling her best friend Sadia about the class. She felt chosen, and also strangely alone, hiding her phone at dinner.
Week 4, Sunday: Sadia's older sister, a college student, saw Parveen flinch at a notification and asked gently. Parveen showed her. That evening they sat with Parveen's Ammi together. Ammi held her hand. "You're not in trouble. An adult asking you to hide things from us is the problem, not you." They blocked him, saved the messages she still had, and reported the account to the class organisers and the cyber-crime helpline that night.

qa.q: Where had their chats moved by Week 3?
qa.a: To a private app.

qa.q: How did Parveen feel by Week 3?
qa.a: Parveen felt chosen and special, but also strangely alone, hiding her phone at dinner and no longer telling Sadia.

qa.q: What protective steps did the family take?
qa.a: Ammi told Parveen she was not in trouble; they blocked Wasim-sir, saved the messages, and reported the account to the organisers and the cyber-crime helpline that night.

qa.q: How did Sadia's older sister help?
qa.a: She noticed Parveen flinch, asked gently, and went with her to Ammi, bringing in a trusted adult the same day.

grounding: Shows a teenager told her bond with an adult is special and must be hidden from her parents, the red flag, and a trusted adult's same-day response.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Class 10, Wednesday.
Alka came in at lunch and asked about "a friend's problem". After a while she said it was hers. For two months she has chatted with "Dev", who says he is seventeen, from a gaming group. He moved their chat to a private app, asked about her home and school, then last week asked for a photo "just for me" and to meet at the mall on Saturday. She said she felt flattered at first and now feels stuck and sick, because she already sent a selfie in her uniform.
I told her clearly that none of this is her fault, and that coming to me was the right thing. She has not replied to him since.
Actions today: informed the safeguarding lead; called her mother, who came at 3 pm; with Alka's agreement we saved the chats, blocked and reported the account, and filed a complaint with the cyber-crime helpline. The Saturday meeting will not happen.
Nirmala

qa.q: Where did Dev ask to meet?
qa.a: At the mall on Saturday.

qa.q: How does Alka feel about the chats now?
qa.a: Alka felt flattered at first but now feels stuck and sick, worried about the selfie she already sent.

qa.q: What did Nirmala do after Alka spoke, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Nirmala told Alka she was not to blame, informed the safeguarding lead, called her mother, and saved, blocked and reported the account the same day, so the meeting will not happen.

qa.q: How might Alka's mother feel arriving at 3 pm?
qa.a: She would likely feel frightened and protective, but also relieved that Alka told someone and the Saturday meeting was stopped.

grounding: Shows a teen whose online contact moved to a private app and asked personal questions, a photo and a meeting, and a counsellor's same-day response that she is not to blame.

passage:
Thursday, late
Sumit sent a voice note tonight saying Naina is the only person who really gets him. Naina doesn't exist. I made her up three months ago, on a lonely night in this new city, with a borrowed photo and a life that sounded brighter than mine. I just wanted someone to reply to me with that kind of excitement.
And he did. He tells her about his exams, his dad's surgery, things his own friends don't know. With every message I feel warm for a minute and then sick. He's trusting a face that isn't mine.
I keep telling myself I'm not like the people who do this for money. But he's still being fooled, whatever my reasons are.
Tomorrow I'll write to him as me, Rekha, and tell him the truth before he shares one more thing. I'm terrified he'll hate me. He has every right to.
And I'm deleting the photo. It was never mine to use.

qa.q: How long ago did Rekha make up Naina?
qa.a: Three months ago.

qa.q: How does Rekha feel reading Sumit's messages?
qa.a: Rekha feels warm for a minute and then sick and guilty, knowing Sumit is trusting a face that isn't Rekha's.

qa.q: What is Rekha planning, and why is it right?
qa.a: Rekha plans to write as Rekha, tell Sumit the truth and delete the borrowed photo, stopping the deception before he shares more.

qa.q: What might Sumit feel when he learns the truth?
qa.a: Sumit may feel hurt, foolish and betrayed, since he shared his exams and his dad's surgery with someone he thought was Naina.

grounding: Shows a lonely young adult who invented an online identity to feel admired, and sees that the other person's trust is being used whatever the motive.

passage: In their Bandra flat, Maria found Madhuri on the balcony floor at midnight, phone face down. For five months Madhuri had talked every night with Neil, an engineer in Dubai. He sent poems, remembered her mother's birthday, and always had a reason not to video call: bad network, a broken camera, a night shift. Tonight Maria's image search, done on a hunch, had shown his photos belonged to a fitness trainer in Brazil. "I planned our wedding in my head," Madhuri whispered. "How can someone so smart be so stupid?" Maria sat down beside her. "You're not stupid. You were kind and honest with someone who wasn't. People who do this practise on thousands." Madhuri cried, for a man who had never existed and for the five months. In the morning Maria stayed with her while she reported the profile and called her elder sister.

qa.q: What reasons did Neil give for not video calling?
qa.a: Bad network, a broken camera and a night shift.

qa.q: What does Madhuri's question about being so stupid reveal?
qa.a: Madhuri feels ashamed as well as grief-stricken, blaming herself while mourning the man and the five months.

qa.q: What is helpful about Maria's response?
qa.a: Maria sits with Madhuri, says being deceived is not stupidity, and stays while Madhuri reports the profile and calls her sister.

qa.q: How might Maria have felt when the search showed the photos belonged to someone else?
qa.a: Maria likely felt worried and sad for Madhuri, knowing the news would hurt, which is why Maria stayed close.

grounding: Shows a young adult who invested feelings in an online partner who avoided video calls, and feels grief and shame when the truth comes out.
